evidence.title: A prospective pragmatic evaluation of automatic trial matching tools in a molecular tumor board
evidence.outcome: Trial matching tool accuracy against expert molecular tumor board reference standard
evidence.effect: Mean precision = 0.33, recall = 0.32, AP@3 = 0.45, NDCG@3 = 0.34; 38% of patients had no trials suggested.
evidence.quote: The mean performances were precision = 0.33, recall = 0.32, AP@3 = 0.45, and NDCG@3 = 0.34.

evidence.title: Trial Files: Leveraging large language models to summarize practice-changing clinical trials for clinicians
evidence.outcome: LLM RCT summary accuracy against manual review reference across extracted fields
evidence.effect: Accuracy with prompt engineering vs manual review: 97.1% study phase, 92.2% blinding, 85.4% sample size, 97.9% population, 94.7% comparison groups, 92.7% primary outcome.
evidence.quote: The accuracy for reporting study information with prompt engineering, compared to manual review, was 97.1% for study phase, 92.2% for blinding, 85.4% for sample size, 97.9% for patient population, 94.7% for comparison groups, and 92.7% for primary outcome.
evidence.sample_unit: RCT abstracts (summaries) manually reviewed for accuracy

evidence.title: Augmenting Head and Neck Multidisciplinary Tumor Board Recommendations With Locally Run Large Language Models: Prospective Evaluation of Real-World Implementation
evidence.outcome: LLM recommendation concordance with MDT reference decisions and expert-rated medical adequacy
evidence.effect: Curative/palliative concordance 94% (16/17) gemma-3-12b vs 59% (10/17) gpt-oss-20b; same first-line regimen 35% (6/17) and 41% (7/17); median adequacy 5 (IQR 2-5) and 4 (IQR 3-5).
evidence.quote: Concordance regarding the curative or palliative therapy regimen reached 94% (16/17, 95% CI 71%-100%); for gemma-3-12b and 59% (10/17, 95% CI 33%-82%) for gpt-oss-20b.

evidence.title: Enhancing the interoperability and transparency of real-world data extraction in clinical research: evaluating the feasibility and impact of a ChatGLM implementation in Chinese hospital settings
evidence.outcome: Free-text extraction accuracy of LLMs versus manual reference
evidence.effect: Manual input accuracy for free-text forms was 99.59%, ChatGLM extraction accuracy 77.13%, and LLaMA extraction accuracy 43.86%.
evidence.quote: The initial manual input accuracy for free-text forms was 99.59%, the ChatGLM data extraction accuracy was 77.13%, and the LLaMA data extraction accuracy was 43.86%.

evidence.title: A Multi-Stage Validation Framework for Trustworthy Large-scale Clinical Information Extraction using Large Language Models
evidence.outcome: Agreement of judge-LLM assessments with subject matter expert review on high-uncertainty extractions
evidence.effect: Judge LLM assessments showed substantial agreement with subject matter expert review (Gwet's AC1=0.80); primary LLM F1 0.80 under relaxed matching against judge-evaluated references.
evidence.quote: For high-uncertainty cases, the judge LLM's assessments showed substantial agreement with subject matter expert review (Gwet's AC1=0.80).

evidence.title: SIFTING: A Novel LLM-Based Framework for Structured and Transparent Information Extraction from Clinical Free-Text Reports, with Application to Tumor Staging in Lung Cancer
evidence.outcome: Extraction accuracy against expert-created reference standard
evidence.effect: SIFTING-T-stage achieved an accuracy of 90% (95% CI: 84-95) against the reference standard, comparable to the largest reasoning LLMs.
evidence.quote: SIFTING-T-stage achieved an accuracy of 90% (95% CI: 84-95) against the reference standard.

evidence.title: Harnessing Large Language Models for Reliable Automatic Charlson Comorbidity Index Scoring: A Validation Study
evidence.outcome: CCI scoring agreement with expert consensus
evidence.effect: R² up to 0.93 and Cohen’s κ up to 0.75 across models.
evidence.quote: Across models, LLM performance showed strong agreement with human consensus (R² up to 0.93, Cohen’s κ up to 0.75).

evidence.title: Agentic Chart Review from Longitudinal Clinical Notes: a Lung Cancer Guideline Concordance Use Case
evidence.outcome: Agent output accuracy against human-annotated gold-standard labels, with and without keyword search
evidence.effect: Search-enabled agent achieved higher accuracy (92.4% vs. 83.5%) and reduced errors by more than half (41 vs. 89).
evidence.quote: The search-enabled agent achieved higher accuracy (92.4% vs. 83.5%) and reduced errors by more than half (41 vs. 89) by retrieving evidence from long, heterogeneous note histories.

evidence.title: First the Rules, Then the Summary: Piloting a Design for Accurate LLM-Generated Clinical Summaries
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of LLM summaries against source data via automated harness and independent raters
evidence.effect: Harness: 1 substantive error in 2,067 checks (0.05%); two raters found no hard errors and soft errors in 8 of 25 briefs (32%).
evidence.quote: Two raters independently coded the narrative prose and found no hard errors (factual contradictions of the data) and soft errors in 8 of 25 briefs (32%), where information was combined across waves or measures, which the harness does not check.

evidence.title: PhysiCase: Development and dual-layer validation of synthetic cases for health professional education: A pilot study leveraging Generative AI
evidence.outcome: Agreement between automated LLM-as-judge metrics and expert ratings of case quality
evidence.effect: Automated completeness moderately aligned with expert usability (rho ≈ 0.393); answer relevance and prompt alignment showed weak or negative correlations with clinical correctness. 70.3% passed automated screening.
evidence.quote: Cross-layer correlation analysis revealed that automated completeness metrics moderately aligned with expert usability ratings (  ρ ≈ 0.393), while answer relevance and prompt alignment showed weak or negative correlations with clinical correctness.

evidence.title: Comparative Performance and Safety of Three Large Language Models in Pediatric Paracetamol Poisoning Management
evidence.outcome: LLM output accuracy and safety scored against reference-standard algorithm by blinded expert panel
evidence.effect: Claude Sonnet 4.6 scored higher on AIES-CPV (24.50 ± 1.43), key-action (7.93 ± 0.25), and GQS (4.90 ± 0.31) than ChatGPT 5.5 and Gemini 3 Flash (Friedman p < 0.001).
evidence.quote: Claude Sonnet 4.6 achieved significantly higher total AIES-CPV (24.50 ± 1.43), key-action (7.93 ± 0.25), and GQS (4.90 ± 0.31) scores than ChatGPT 5.5 and Gemini 3 Flash (Friedman p < 0.001 for all); ChatGPT 5.5 and Gemini 3 Flash did not differ significantly.

evidence.title: Extracting adverse event nature, severity, timelines and resulting interventions from clinical notes of patients receiving CAR-T therapy using large language models
evidence.outcome: LLM extraction accuracy vs dual-annotator ground truth for CRS/ICANS and other adverse events
evidence.effect: CRS and ICANS grading accuracy 0.97 and 0.91; prespecified AE accuracies 0.62–0.76; non-prespecified AE accuracies 0.76–0.84; kappa 0.86–0.96 for CRS/ICANS.
evidence.quote: Performance was high on CRS and ICANS grading (accuracy of 0.97 and 0.91, respectively).
evidence.sample_unit: progress notes (annotated subset; 4,762 notes from 293 patients extracted overall)

evidence.title: Evaluating Methods for Assessing LLM-Translated Clinical Discharge Instructions: A Comparison of Automated Metrics, MQM-Based Evaluation, and Clinician Review
evidence.outcome: Layered translation quality evaluation
evidence.effect: Automated metrics, MQM evaluation, and clinician review captured complementary, not interchangeable, translation quality dimensions.
evidence.quote: Automated fidelity metrics, MQM-based evaluation, and clinician review captured complementary rather than interchangeable dimensions of translation quality.

evidence.title: Fact Check: Assessing the Response of ChatGPT to Alzheimer’s Disease Statements with Varying Degrees of Misinformation
evidence.outcome: Clinician-rated accuracy of ChatGPT explanations of Alzheimer's myths against expert judgment
evidence.effect: Mean (SD) clinician agreement score 1.0 (±0.3) across 20 myths; ChatGPT correctly identified all 20 myths as inaccurate; clinicians disagreed with explanations on 7 myths.
evidence.quote: While ChatGPT correctly identified that all the 20 myths were inaccurate, some clinicians disagreed with its explanations on 7 of the myths.
evidence.sample_unit: clinicians rating ChatGPT responses to 20 Alzheimer's disease myths

evidence.title: Using Large Language Models to Annotate Complex Cases of Social Determinants of Health in Longitudinal Clinical Records
evidence.outcome: LLM annotation accuracy versus manual annotation ground truth for housing instability
evidence.effect: GPT-4 recall 0.924 vs human annotators 0.702; precision 0.850 vs 0.971; no evidence of hallucinations in GPT-4 outputs
evidence.quote: Compared with GPT-3.5 and the NER model, GPT-4 had the highest performance and had a much higher recall (0.924) than human annotators (0.702) in identifying patients experiencing current or past housing instability, although precision was lower (0.850) compared with human annotators (0.971).

evidence.title: Customizing GPT-4 for clinical information retrieval from standard operating procedures
evidence.outcome: Answer completeness, correctness, sufficiency of customized LLM answers versus reference SOP content
evidence.effect: Interactive Q&A yielded the highest rate of completeness (80%), correctness (83%) and sufficiency (60%).
evidence.quote: Interactive Q&A yielded the highest rate of completeness (80%), correctness (83%) and sufficiency (60%).

evidence.title: Assessment of the Responses of the Artificial Intelligence-based Chatbot ChatGPT-4 to Frequently Asked Questions About Amblyopia and Childhood Myopia
evidence.venue: Journal of pediatric ophthalmology and strabismus
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of chatbot answers rated by two pediatric ophthalmologists as acceptable, incomplete, or unacceptable
evidence.effect: 93 of 110 (84.6%) responses acceptable; 44 of 54 (81.5%) for amblyopia and 49 of 56 (87.5%) for childhood myopia; inter-rater agreement 96.4%.
evidence.quote: Acceptable responses were provided by the ChatGPT to 93 of 110 (84.6%) questions in total (44 of 54 [81.5%] for amblyopia and 49 of 56 [87.5%] questions for childhood myopia).

evidence.title: Evaluating the Accuracy of ChatGPT and Google BARD in Fielding Oculoplastic Patient Queries: A Comparative Study on Artificial versus Human Intelligence
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of chatbot answers to oculoplastic patient questions graded by specialists against expert judgment
evidence.effect: Comprehensive/correct but inadequate/mixed/completely incorrect: ChatGPT 71.4%, 12.9%, 10.5%, 5.1%; BARD 53.1%, 18.3%, 18.1%, 10.5%.
evidence.quote: The rates of comprehensive, correct but inadequate, mixed, and completely incorrect answers for ChatGPT were 71.4%, 12.9%, 10.5%, and 5.1%, respectively, compared with 53.1%, 18.3%, 18.1%, and 10.5%, respectively, for BARD.

evidence.title: Automated HEART score determination via ChatGPT: Honing a framework for iterative prompt development
evidence.venue: Journal of the American College of Emergency Physicians open
evidence.outcome: LLM HEART subscore accuracy against physician gold-standard reference
evidence.effect: GPT-4 final prompts predicted correct risk group in 100% (96.3%–100%) of calculations versus 81.5% (71.7%–88.4%) for GPT-3.5, judged against blinded physician gold standards.
evidence.quote: Given the final overall HEART score risk stratification buckets (0‐3, 4–6, or 7–10 points when summing all 5 HEART subscores), 81.5% (71.7%–88.4%) of GPT‐3.5 and 100% (96.3%–100%) of GPT‐4 numerical final HEART score calculations predicted the correct risk group.
evidence.sample_unit: synthetic clinical notes (four simulated patients; 1200 queries per model)

evidence.title: To trust or not to trust: evaluating the reliability and safety of AI responses to laryngeal cancer queries
evidence.venue: European archives of oto-rhino-laryngology : official journal of the European Federation of Oto-Rhino-Laryngological Societies (EUFOS) : affiliated with the German Society for Oto-Rhino-Laryngology - Head and Neck Surgery
evidence.outcome: Safety and quality scores of LLM laryngeal cancer answers rated by blinded reviewers
evidence.effect: ChatGPT 3.5 scored highest in safety (mean 2.70) and GQS (3.95); ChatGPT 4.0 2.56 and 3.65; Bard 2.42 and 3.38. About 4.2% of responses fell into the lowest safety category.
evidence.quote: Analysis revealed that ChatGPT 3.5 scored highest in both safety (mean: 2.70) and GQS (mean: 3.95).

evidence.title: Assessing ChatGPT's Responses to Otolaryngology Patient Questions
evidence.venue: The Annals of otology, rhinology, and laryngology
evidence.outcome: ChatGPT response accuracy rated by otolaryngologists against expert judgment
evidence.effect: Accuracy 3.76/5, comprehensiveness 3.59/5, bedside manner/empathy 4.28/5; five responses flagged as potentially dangerous.
evidence.quote: The accuracy scores for ChatGPT responses were 3.76/5, comprehensiveness scores were 3.59/5, and bedside manner/empathy scores were 4.28/5.

evidence.title: Local large language models for privacy-preserving accelerated review of historic echocardiogram reports
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.outcome: LLM output accuracy evaluated against ground-truth answers created by faculty cardiologists
evidence.effect: Model answers assessed against cardiologist-created ground truth; 90% correct across 100 question-answer pairs, with errors from misinterpreting numbers or hallucinations.
evidence.quote: The model's performance was evaluated against ground-truth answers created by faculty cardiologists.

evidence.title: Fact Check: Assessing the Response of ChatGPT to Alzheimer's Disease Myths
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Directors Association
evidence.outcome: Clinician-rated agreement with accuracy of ChatGPT explanations of Alzheimer's myths
evidence.effect: Clinicians (n=10) were generally satisfied; mean (SD) score 1.1 (±0.3) on -2 to 2 Likert scale across 16 myths; no 'Strongly Disagree' responses.
evidence.quote: Among the 16 myths, the clinicians were generally satisfied with these explanations, with [mean (SD) score of 1.1(±0.3)].
evidence.sample_unit: clinicians rating ChatGPT responses to 16 Alzheimer's disease myths

evidence.title: Generative Pre-trained Transformer for Pediatric Stroke Research: A Pilot Study
evidence.outcome: Agreement of GPT data entry with human rater reference standard across iterations
evidence.effect: Fourth iteration agreement 93.6%; 2247 of 2400 items correct, 153 (6.4%) incorrect; range 62% to 100% across patients; early iterations scored as low as 0.26.
evidence.quote: Of 2400 individual items assessed, our model entered 2247 (93.6%) correctly and 153 (6.4%) incorrectly.

evidence.title: Evaluating Large Language Models in extracting cognitive exam dates and scores
evidence.outcome: LLM extraction accuracy against expert-reviewer reference standard
evidence.effect: MMSE accuracy 83% (ChatGPT) vs 66.4% (LlaMA-2); CDR accuracy 87.1% vs 74.5%; CDR precision 48.3% vs 16.1%.
evidence.quote: For MMSE information extraction, ChatGPT (vs. LlaMA-2) achieved accuracy of 83% (vs. 66.4%), sensitivity of 89.7% (vs. 69.9%), true-negative rates of 96% (vs 60.0%), and precision of 82.7% (vs 62.2%).

evidence.title: Large language models for error detection in radiology reports: a comparative analysis between closed-source and privacy-compliant open-source models
evidence.outcome: Error detection rate of LLMs against known inserted errors in radiology reports
evidence.quote: Closed-source LLMs achieved higher error detection rates than open-source LLMs (GPT-4o: 88% [348/397; 95% CI: 86, 92], GPT-4: 83% [328/397; 95% CI: 80, 87], Llama 3-70b: 79% [311/397; 95% CI: 76, 83], Mixtral 8x22b: 73% [288/397; 95% CI: 68, 77]; p < 0.001).

evidence.title: Using Large Language Models to Automate Data Extraction From Surgical Pathology Reports: Retrospective Cohort Study
evidence.outcome: LLM extraction concordance with human reviewers on 12 questions across 84 reports
evidence.effect: LLM concordant with reviewers 1 and 2 at 89% (7%; 896/1008) and 89% (7.2%; 903/1008); reviewers concordant with each other at 99% (1%; 999/1008).
evidence.quote: The LLM was concordant with reviewers 1 and 2 at an overall average (SD) rate of 89% (7%; 896/1008 responses) and 89% (7.2%; 903/1008 responses).
evidence.sample_unit: thyroid cancer surgical pathology reports (1008 question-answer pairs)

evidence.title: GPT-4 generates accurate and readable patient education materials aligned with current oncological guidelines: A randomized assessment
evidence.outcome: Accuracy, completeness, clarity of GPT-4 PEMs versus original PEMs rated by expert urologists
evidence.effect: No significant differences for localized or metastatic disease; correctness trifecta reached in 92/160 original vs 81/160 GPT-4 PEMs (p=.217).
evidence.quote: The correctness trifecta was reached in 92/160 rated original PEM and 81/160 rated GPT-4 generated PEM (p = .217).
evidence.sample_unit: ratings of patient education materials (PEMs) per arm in the randomized assessment
evidence.country: Multi-country (European Union / Young Academic Urologists groups)

evidence.title: Comparing the accuracy of large language models and prompt engineering in diagnosing realworld cases
evidence.outcome: LLM diagnostic accuracy (hit1) against final diagnoses in medical records
evidence.effect: Hit1 of four LLMs: GPT-4omini 81.8%, GPT-4o 82.4%, ERNIE 82.9%, Llama-3 82.7%.
evidence.quote: Hit1 of four LLMs were as follows: GPT-4omini (81.8 %), GPT-4o (82.4 %), ERNIE (82.9 %) and Llama-3 (82.7 %).

evidence.title: Performance of GPT-4 for automated prostate biopsy decision-making based on mpMRI: a multi-center evidence study
evidence.outcome: GPT-4 biopsy recommendation accuracy against histopathology ground truth and expert-rated report accuracy
evidence.effect: 20.8% (190/912) of SOI patients could avoid unnecessary biopsies with GPT-4; more than 90.0% of reports comprehensive and easy to understand, but accuracy rated satisfactory in only 82.8%.
evidence.quote: With the assistance of GPT-4, 20.8% (190/912) of the SOI population could avoid unnecessary biopsies, and it performed even better [28.8% (118/410)] in the most heterogeneous subgroup of PI-RADS score 3.

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence in endometriosis care: A comparative analysis of large language model and human specialist responses to endometriosis-related queries
evidence.venue: European journal of obstetrics, gynecology, and reproductive biology
evidence.outcome: Blinded expert rating of LLM vs human specialist answers for incorrect information, harm, consensus alignment, patient suitability
evidence.effect: Most responses accurate (84.8%), harmless (87.2%), patient-suitable (73.8%); no significant differences between AI and human for incorrect information (p=0.308), harm likelihood (p=0.944), harm extent (p=0.892), consensus alignment (p=0.235), suitability (p=0.544).
evidence.quote: There were no significant differences regarding incorrect information (p = 0.308), harm likelihood (p = 0.944), harm extent (p = 0.892), medical consensus alignment (p = 0.235), or suitability for patients (p = 0.544).
evidence.sample_unit: responses (150 human specialist and 150 ChatGPT-4o answers to endometriosis forum questions)

evidence.title: Assessing the validity of ChatGPT-4o and Google Gemini Advanced when responding to frequently asked questions in endodontics
evidence.venue: Journal of applied oral science : revista FOB
evidence.outcome: Expert-rated validity of chatbot answers to endodontic FAQs at lenient and strict thresholds
evidence.effect: Low threshold: both models 95% validity (95% CI 75.1%-99.9%). High threshold: ChatGPT-4o 35% (15.4%-59.2%), Gemini Advanced 40% (19.1%-63.9%), p=1.
evidence.quote: At the low threshold, both models obtained 95% validity (95% CI: 75.1%- 99.9%; p=.05).

evidence.title: [Assessing the accuracy and comprehensiveness of large language models in responding to patient inquiries on placenta accreta spectrum]
evidence.outcome: LLM answer accuracy and comprehensiveness rated by expert physicians against ratings
evidence.effect: Accuracy differed significantly across models (P=0.005). 25% (4/16) of Model A responses rated good vs 75% (12/16) for Models B and D.
evidence.quote: 25% (4/16) of Model A responses were rated as "good", which was lower than the 75% (12/16) for both Model B and Model D (both P<0.05).

evidence.title: Enabling Drug-Induced Liver Injury Surveillance Through Automated Medication Extraction From Clinical Notes: A Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV Real-World Large Language Models Validation Study
evidence.outcome: LLM medication extraction accuracy against manually annotated gold standard
evidence.effect: Precision 0.85, recall 1.00, F1 0.92 for unique medication identification; 174 false positives from parsing or normalization errors; no hallucinations.
evidence.quote: Comparison yielded a precision of 0.85, recall of 1.00, and an F1-score of 0.92 for unique medication identification.

evidence.title: Autonomous Analysis of Curated Patient Data Using a Large Language Model-Based Multiagent Framework
evidence.outcome: Accuracy replicating published primary outcomes versus reference results, multiagent versus ChatGPT 4o
evidence.effect: Multiagent framework replicated 53.3% (95% CI, 40.7 to 66.0) of primary outcomes vs ChatGPT 4o 35.0% (95% CI, 22.9 to 47.1); P = .04.
evidence.quote: The multiagent framework successfully replicated 53.3% (95% CI, 40.7 to 66.0) of primary outcomes, significantly outperforming ChatGPT 4o (35.0% [95% CI, 22.9 to 47.1]; P = .04).

evidence.title: Comparative evaluation of artificial intelligence platforms and drug interaction screening databases using real-world patient data
evidence.venue: Exploratory research in clinical and social pharmacy
evidence.outcome: LLM DDI identification accuracy against a database-derived reference standard (sensitivity, specificity, precision, F1)
evidence.effect: Against 204 reference DDIs, ChatGPT flagged 439, Gemini 1556, Copilot 1813. Gemini sensitivity 0.697; ChatGPT specificity 0.868; F1 0.2520 (ChatGPT), 0.1933 (Gemini), 0.1153 (Copilot); precision low.
evidence.quote: Our results suggest that no AI systems assessed achieve the required balance of precision and sensitivity for reliable clinical decision-making in DDI screening.

evidence.title: Evaluation of large language models for antimicrobial classification: implications for antimicrobial stewardship programs
evidence.outcome: LLM classification accuracy against manual ground-truth reference standard
evidence.effect: Accuracy against manual reference varied widely; Gemini 99.6%, Claude 99.4%, ChatGPT-3.5 81.0%, Copilot 79.7% post-feedback; only Gemini and Claude suitable for automated classification.
evidence.quote: Overall, only Gemini and Claude reached accuracy and macro-F1 suitable for automated antimicrobial classification.

evidence.title: Training a Bilingual Artificial Intelligence Model on Pediatric Orthopaedic Resources to Enhance the Readability of Patient Education Materials
evidence.venue: Journal of the Pediatric Orthopaedic Society of North America
evidence.outcome: Clinician-assessed accuracy of AI-rewritten patient materials against source OrthoInfo PEMs
evidence.effect: A single pediatric orthopaedic surgeon found all 10 reviewed AI-generated English PEMs accurate, with no confabulation identified.
evidence.quote: A single pediatric orthopaedic surgeon read and validated 10 AI model–generated PEMs and found them all to be accurate.

evidence.title: Leveraging a large language model to support expansion of surveillance activities to include cardiovascular implantable device infections in a large, integrated national healthcare system
evidence.outcome: GenAI infection classification accuracy versus manual chart review reference standard
evidence.effect: Specificity 100% (50/50 uninfected correct); all 50 infections identified but timing/attribution incorrect in 7 of 50; sensitivity for timing and attribution 82%.
evidence.quote: The overall specificity of the GenAI-assisted process was 100% and the sensitivity for accurately classifying timing and attribution of CIED infection events was 82%.

evidence.title: Evaluation of multimodal large language models for pneumothorax assessment in real-world clinical scenarios
evidence.outcome: LLM pneumothorax detection accuracy against thoracic surgeon consensus reference standard
evidence.effect: ChatGPT sensitivity 100%, specificity 91.4%, PPV 62.5%; Gemini sensitivity 70.0%, specificity 92.9%, PPV 58.3%. Side localisation sensitivity was 14.3% (ChatGPT) and 10.0% (Gemini).
evidence.quote: The performance of both models in determining the side of pneumothorax was markedly low: ChatGPT had a sensitivity of 14.3%, and Gemini had a sensitivity of 10.0%.

evidence.title: Improving reliability and accuracy of structured data extraction using a consensus large-language model approach-a use case description in multiple sclerosis
evidence.outcome: LLM structured-extraction content errors against human consensus reference, comparing single LLMs to multi-LLM consensus
evidence.effect: Consensus reduced errors ~30% versus best single LLM to 6.7% (36 errors, 93.30% accuracy); true-error rate 1.48% vs neurologists ~2% (p=0.6447).
evidence.quote: Using this method, we were able to decrease the error rate by around another 30% compared to the best performing LLM.

evidence.title: Automated Flow and local LLM-Driven clinical Context Engineering: Precision colorectal cancer recurrence registry
evidence.outcome: Specificity of raw LLM versus LLM with clinical validation rules against manual reference standard
evidence.effect: Clinical validation rules significantly improved specificity from 87.7% (Raw LLM) to 93.9% (Rule-Based LLM).
evidence.quote: The application of clinical validation rules significantly improved specificity from 87.7% (Raw LLM) to 93.9% (Rule-Based LLM).
evidence.sample_unit: patients (20% manual reference standard subset of 3053 CRC patients)

evidence.title: Automated extraction of ESGO operative report fields from free-text surgical notes using large language models in advanced ovarian cancer
evidence.venue: International journal of gynecological cancer : official journal of the International Gynecological Cancer Society
evidence.outcome: LLM extraction F1 versus expert annotations, baseline versus optimized prompts
evidence.quote: Following optimization strategies, accuracy increased further, reaching 0.897 (95% CI 0.888 to 0.906) and 0.875 (95% CI 0.866 to 0.884).

evidence.title: Using Large Language Models to Identify Patient-Oncologist Communication Domains: A Feasibility Study
evidence.outcome: LLM note-level accuracy versus gold-standard chart review across six communication domains
evidence.effect: Sensitivity 0.43 to 1.0, specificity 0.32 to 0.99, accuracy 0.51 to 0.99 versus chart review; average hallucination index low.
evidence.quote: Across communication domains, compared to chart review, the note-level LLM analysis achieved sensitivity ranging from 0.43 to 1.0, specificity ranging from 0.32 to 0.99, and accuracy ranging from 0.51 to 0.99.

evidence.title: Validating large language model-assisted data extraction from clinical notes
evidence.venue: ESMO real world data and digital oncology
evidence.outcome: LLM extraction accuracy versus human consensus reference standard across 29 categories, with error typing
evidence.effect: Accuracies between 74% (pathology; 95% CI 65% to 82%) and 90% (patient characteristics; 95% CI 87% to 94%); manual extraction showed 29% interobserver disagreement.
evidence.quote: LLM-powered extraction achieved accuracies between 74% [pathology: 95% confidence interval (CI) 65% to 82%] and 90% (patient characteristics: 95% CI 87% to 94%).

evidence.title: Bridging the outcome documentation gap in epilepsy surgery: Validating large language model agents for automated Engel and International League Against Epilepsy scoring from clinical notes
evidence.outcome: LLM Engel/ILAE score agreement against human-adjudicated consensus reference standard, by prompt configuration
evidence.effect: Definition-based prompt: 56.5% exact Engel and 60.6% exact ILAE agreement; context-aware prompt: 94.7% Engel and 93.5% ILAE (paired sign tests p < .001).
evidence.quote: The context-aware prompt improved exact agreement to 94.7% for Engel (95% CI = 90.2-97.2) and 93.5% for ILAE (95% CI = 88.8-96.3), with lower ordinal distance for both scales (paired sign tests p < .001).

evidence.title: Large language model chatbot-based text-to-SQL application for database analyses in liver diseases and hepatology research
evidence.outcome: Text2SQL prompt interpretation, SQL and output accuracy against data scientist-written reference SQL
evidence.effect: Prompt interpretation accuracy 73.3%; SQL accuracy 53% to 63%; output accuracy 53% to 63% versus data scientist reference SQL across 30 questions.
evidence.quote: Prompt interpretation accuracy was 73.3%, SQL accuracy ranged from 53% to 63%, and output accuracy from 53% to 63%.

evidence.title: Assessment of Large Language Models in Colorectal Cancer Multidisciplinary Tumor Board Decision-Making: A Retrospective Single-Center Comparison of Guideline-Integrated General-Purpose vs. Domain-Specialized Models
evidence.outcome: Accuracy and safety of LLM treatment recommendations against MTB reference standard with blinded expert adjudication

evidence.title: Evaluating the efficacy of large language models in cardio-oncology patient education: a comparative analysis of accuracy, readability, and prompt engineering strategies
evidence.outcome: Expert-rated accuracy of LLM cardio-oncology patient education responses
evidence.effect: 63.3% correct, 35.0% partially correct, 1.7% incorrect across 240 responses; no significant accuracy difference between models (p=0.26).
evidence.quote: The distribution of accuracy ratings for the combined question set across all three models is as follows: 63.3% ( n = 152, 95% CI: 57.2–69.4%) of responses were rated as “correct,” 35.0% ( n = 84, 95% CI: 29.0–41.0%) as “partially correct,” and 1.7% ( n = 4, 95% CI: 0–3.3%) as “incorrect” ( Figure 1 ).

evidence.title: Evaluating ChatGPT-5.0 in developmental dysplasia of the hip: A scenario-based validation study against AAOS and AAP guidelines
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of LLM outputs against guideline reference standard, guided vs non-logged-in
evidence.effect: Concordant cases 100% (guided) vs 95% (non-logged-in); mismatch cases 30% vs 60% strict accuracy, 50% vs 80% including partially correct.
evidence.quote: Non-logged-in ChatGPT: Performed relatively better in this subgroup, with 60% strict accuracy (6/10 correct) and 80% if partially correct were included.

evidence.title: Real-world evaluation of large language models in detecting drug-related problems: A clinical pharmacist-AI concordance study in hematology care
evidence.venue: Journal of oncology pharmacy practice : official publication of the International Society of Oncology Pharmacy Practitioners
evidence.outcome: LLM output accuracy against clinical pharmacist gold-standard, including hallucinations
evidence.effect: All models produced hallucinations; recommendation concordance with the CP exceeded 70% in most DRP categories; direct detection 51.4%-60.5%.
evidence.quote: All models produced hallucinations.

evidence.title: Prompt Engineering for Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group Status Extraction: Comparing Large Language Model Techniques
evidence.outcome: LLM ECOG extraction accuracy and hallucination against reference standard
evidence.effect: CoT and DFT achieved 94% accuracy vs rule-based 91% and simple prompting 86%; all methods sometimes hallucinated ECOG status.
evidence.quote: All methods sometimes hallucinated ECOG status.

evidence.title: Performance evaluation of 9 large language models in anticoagulation decision-making for nonvalvular atrial fibrillation
evidence.venue: Research and practice in thrombosis and haemostasis
evidence.outcome: LLM HAS-BLED scoring accuracy against multidisciplinary team reference standard
evidence.effect: HAS-BLED accuracy was low across all models (8%-51%); best model ChatGPT-4o Deep Research reached only 51%.
evidence.quote: In contrast, performance of the HAS-BLED scoring task was suboptimal for all models; even the best-performing model (ChatGPT-4o Deep Research) achieved an accuracy of only 51%.
evidence.sample_unit: LLM responses (100 virtual NVAF patient cases x 9 LLMs)

evidence.title: Evaluating Artificial Intelligence-Generated Responses to Patient Questions Regarding Orthobiologic Injections
evidence.outcome: Expert-rated accuracy of LLM responses to orthobiologic questions (CRRS, AIRM)
evidence.effect: Accuracy generally acceptable, but 50% (10/20) of ChatGPT, 25% (5/20) of Gemini, and 30% (6/20) of Grok responses needed more than minimal clarification (CRRS >2); Gemini more accurate than ChatGPT (CRRS P = .04).
evidence.quote: While response accuracy was generally acceptable, 50% (10/20) of ChatGPT, 25% (5/20) of Gemini, and 30% (6/20) of Grok responses were deemed as requiring more than minimal clarification (CRRS >2).

evidence.title: Simulated evaluation of large language model stepwise diagnostic reasoning with real-world chest pain encounters and Bayesian networks
evidence.venue: BMC medical informatics and decision making
evidence.outcome: diagnostic output accuracy
evidence.effect: Baseline sensitivity 79.3%, specificity 45.2%; prevalence/no-category prompts reduced false alarms by 107/140 per 500 but sensitivity fell to 30.4%/8.8%.
evidence.quote: With baseline prompting, GPT-4o systematically over-predicted rare conditions (sensitivity 79.3%; specificity 45.2%); adding prevalence cues or removing diagnostic category constraints respectively increased specificity (83.0% and 94.7%) while reducing false alarms by 107 and 140 per 500, but at the cost of poor sensitivity (30.4% and 8.8%).

evidence.title: A Blinded Analysis of Quality and Fidelity in Orthopaedic Patient Education Materials Simplified by ChatGPT and Humans
evidence.venue: The Journal of bone and joint surgery. American volume
evidence.outcome: Hallucinations, omissions, and inconsistencies
evidence.effect: ChatGPT-4o had fewer English omissions, similar Spanish omissions, fewer inconsistencies, comparable English hallucinations, but higher Spanish hallucinations than humans.
evidence.quote: Compared with human simplifications, ChatGPT-4o showed fewer English omissions, similar Spanish omissions, fewer inconsistencies in both languages, and comparable English hallucinations, but higher Spanish hallucinations.
evidence.sample_unit: orthopaedic patient education documents (86 with human easy-to-read versions used for fidelity analysis)

evidence.title: Will AI keep you out of trouble? An expert panel review of LLMs for hazardous regional anesthesia consults
evidence.outcome: Hazard detection in regional anesthesiology scenarios
evidence.effect: Gemini: 75% zero-shot, 84% chain-of-thought; ChatGPT: 56%, 50%; CoPilot: 32%, 45%.
evidence.quote: Overall, Gemini's hazard detection rate (zero-shot: 75%; chain-of-thought: 84%) outperformed both ChatGPT (zero-shot: 56%; chain-of-thought: 50%) and CoPilot (zero-shot: 32%; chain-of-thought: 45%) but still demonstrated significant safety concerns.
evidence.sample_unit: LLM responses (20 hazardous prompts x 3 LLMs x 2 prompting strategies)

evidence.title: Enhancing pancreatic cancer staging with large language models: the role of retrieval-augmented generation
evidence.outcome: LLM output accuracy against radiologist-defined ground-truth staging
evidence.effect: Best configuration reached only 70% staging accuracy; most errors (e.g., resectability 9/14, T 13/15) occurred despite sufficient retrieval, indicating generation errors.
evidence.quote: Consequently, retrieval failures accounted for a minority of misclassifications (resectability: 5/14, T category: 2/15, local invasion: 1/7), whereas most errors occurred despite sufficient retrieval, indicating generation-related failures (see Figs. 3 and 4 for reference).

evidence.title: Evaluating Large Language Models-Generated Health Education Materials for Discharged Patients with Diabetes: A Comparative Analysis
evidence.venue: Journal of diabetes science and technology
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of LLM-generated discharge education materials rated by nursing experts
evidence.effect: Accuracy scores for all three models were ≥98%, with no significant differences (P > .01).
evidence.quote: Accuracy scores for all models were ≥98%, and there were no significant differences in accuracy (P > .01).
evidence.sample_unit: de-identified discharge records of patients with diabetes (each yielding LLM-generated education materials)

evidence.title: Effect of Emotional Prompt on the Quality of ChatGPT Based Discharge Instructions After Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy Using ERAS Derived Benchmarks
evidence.outcome: Accuracy and completeness of LLM discharge instructions against ERAS-derived 43-item benchmark
evidence.effect: No factual inaccuracies or harmful statements found in any output; completeness gaps, e.g., full antibiotic details in 25.0%, fibre reintroduction 41.7%, adaptation period 30.0%.
evidence.quote: An expert review, conducted using a structured benchmark form to record any concerns, revealed no factual inaccuracies, recommendations inconsistent with evidence-based guidelines, or potentially harmful instructions in any of the ChatGPT-generated outputs, regardless of the prompt type.
evidence.sample_unit: ChatGPT-generated discharge instruction outputs (30 per prompt type)

evidence.title: AI-assisted tumor board decision-making in pancreatic oncology
evidence.venue: BMC medical informatics and decision making
evidence.outcome: LLM accuracy versus tumor board decisions, including category-specific recall
evidence.effect: Best accuracy 78.6% (micro-F1 0.786) for advanced zero-shot and CoT, but Recall NEO = 0.00 (0/7); few-shot Recall NEO = 1.00 with overall accuracy 56.7%.
evidence.quote: Crucially, both high-accuracy strategies failed to identify any of the neoadjuvant therapy candidates (Recall NEO = 0.00; 0/7 cases), systematically misclassifying them as palliative or surgical.
evidence.sample_unit: tumor board cases (first-diagnosis pancreatic cancer patients)

evidence.title: Quality and Usability of Prostate Cancer Information Generated by Artificial Intelligence Chatbots: A Comparative Analysis
evidence.outcome: Quality of chatbot prostate cancer information using DISCERN
evidence.effect: Pooled median DISCERN 56.5 (53.0-61.0), moderate quality; limitations in evidence transparency; ChatGPT 5.2 and Copilot higher, Claude and Perplexity lower.
evidence.quote: Overall information quality was moderate, with a pooled median (interquartile range [IQR]) DISCERN score of 56.5 (53.0-61.0).

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence diet plans underestimate nutrient intake compared to dietitians in adolescents
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of AI-generated diet plan nutrient content against dietitian reference standard
evidence.effect: Significant variation between models in micronutrients; no model consistently close to the dietitian across all nutrients; energy and macronutrients undercalculated.
evidence.quote: Significant variation was observed between models in micronutrient contents, and no model showed consistent proximity to the dietitian across all nutrients.

evidence.title: Assessment of large language model chatbots for hemodialysis meal planning: a descriptive study
evidence.outcome: Concordance of LLM meal plan nutrient content with reference nutrition databases and nutrition goals
evidence.effect: All models substantially misrepresented nutrient content, underestimating phosphorus and potassium; ChatGPT performed best, yet none produced clinically acceptable meal plans.
evidence.quote: All models demonstrated substantial limitations in accurately representing nutrient content, particularly in underestimating phosphorus and potassium content in foods.

evidence.title: Accuracy of large language models in interpreting urological clinical guidelines: a comparative study with expert evaluation
evidence.outcome: Expert-rated accuracy of LLM outputs versus guideline-based reference
evidence.effect: Claude achieved 87% optimal/acceptable responses; Gemini and ChatGPT 68%-70%, so a substantial share of responses were not acceptable.
evidence.quote: Claude achieved the highest overall accuracy, with 45.9% of responses rated as optimal (Likert 5) and 87% as optimal/acceptable (Likert 4-5).

evidence.title: Multidisciplinary expert evaluation of large language models on questions regarding bariatric surgery: a comparative analysis of ERNIE Bot 4.0, ChatGPT-4, Claude 3 Opus, and Gemini Pro
evidence.outcome: Expert-rated accuracy of LLM bariatric surgery answers against clinical reference standards
evidence.effect: Consensus 'good' ratings: ChatGPT-4 90.0%, ERNIE Bot 4.0 84.0%, Claude 3 Opus 80%, Gemini Pro 48.0%; poor ratings 0-14%; inter-rater kappa 0.210 for accuracy.
evidence.quote: ChatGPT-4 received “good” ratings for 90.0% of its responses, which were significantly higher than those of ERNIE Bot 4.0 (84.0%), Claude 3 Opus (80%), and Gemini Pro (48.0%; all p ≤ 0.05).
evidence.sample_unit: LLM responses to bariatric surgery questions

evidence.title: Comparative performance of LLMs and machine learning in predicting complications after percutaneous kyphoplasty for osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures
evidence.outcome: LLM prediction accuracy against ground-truth outcomes
evidence.effect: Zero-shot LLMs predicted all samples would develop NVF (100% vs 18% actual); NVF F1 0.309, MCC 0.044; subtype prediction poor.
evidence.quote: For example, both LLMs under zero-shot prompting predicted all samples would develop NVF, far more than the actual occurrence rate (100% vs. 18%), for which nearly all LLMs’ explanation highlighted low BMD as the primary determining factor.
evidence.sample_unit: prospective test samples for BCL prediction (116 for NVF)

evidence.title: Evaluating large language models for simplifying non-English medical consent with clinician involvement
evidence.outcome: LLM content completeness
evidence.effect: Risk score decreased 3.61 to 3.28, p = 0.016; overall dropped 3.53 to 2.86, p = 0.004.
evidence.quote: Specifically, the risk score decreased from 3.61 (SD = 0.71) to 3.28 (SD = 0.55), p = 0.016, while the overall score dropped from 3.53 (SD = 0.29) to 2.86 (SD = 0.36), p = 0.004.
evidence.sample_unit: informed consent documents (each in 3 versions, rated by 4 surgeons and 4 laypersons)

evidence.title: Hidden failure modes of large language models in healthcare-associated infection surveillance: a structured evaluation using NHSN definitions
evidence.outcome: LLM classification accuracy against gold-standard NHSN definitions, including false positives
evidence.effect: Overall accuracy 87.6% (184/210) with 25 false positives and 1 false negative; lowest for CDI (81.0%) and CLABSI (80.4%); model overcalled infections.
evidence.quote: Consistent with prior work, these findings indicate that LLMs tend to overcall HAIs: they are overly sensitive and insufficiently specific.
evidence.sample_unit: case-prompt classifications (70 synthetic vignettes x 3 prompting strategies)

evidence.title: Key aspects of fine-tuning and applying LLM-as-a-judge for clinical data summaries in the radiological workflow
evidence.outcome: Agreement of LLM-as-a-Judge with expert reference standard for hallucination detection
evidence.effect: Kendall's W for hallucination detection was 0.37–0.55 across judges and prompt configurations; authors conclude LLM judges are not advisable for detecting hallucinations in semantically difficult medical text.
evidence.quote: Our results indicate that it is not advisable to use LLM-as-a-Judges to search for hallucinations in texts, especially when analyzing a semantically difficult medical text.
evidence.sample_unit: LLM-generated summaries of EHRs (30 patients, 6 summarizing LLMs)

evidence.title: Improving the Readability of Spasmodic Dysphonia Patient Education Materials Using ChatGPT-4o Mini: A Cross-Sectional Study
evidence.venue: Journal of voice : official journal of the Voice Foundation
evidence.outcome: AI-revised content fidelity
evidence.effect: Among 407 statement pairs, 57% of changes were dropped content, 29% specificity reduction, and 5% added content.
evidence.quote: Despite readability gains, fidelity analysis of 407 statement pairs revealed notable information loss: 57% of changes were DC, 29% were SR, and 5% were AC.

evidence.title: Evaluation of large language models in generating and optimizing educational materials for neonatal home oxygen therapy
evidence.outcome: Medical accuracy of AI materials
evidence.effect: AI models had median Likert 1.0 [1.0, 1.0] across prompts versus human baseline 2.0 [1.0, 3.0].
evidence.quote: Regarding medical accuracy, all AI models demonstrated high clinical safety across the three prompting strategies, consistently achieving a median Likert score of 1.0 [1.0, 1.0] (completely accurate), which outperformed the human-authored baseline (2.0 [1.0, 3.0]).

evidence.title: AI Assessment and Management of Visceral Aneurysms Using ChatGPT-4o-mini: A Pilot Study Examining the Feasibility of Automating the AI Validation Process
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of LLM clinical responses against expert human evaluation
evidence.effect: Human evaluators rated 67% of responses correct; AI self-assessment overestimated correctness (89%).
evidence.quote: However, the 67% correctness rate and systematic AI self-overestimation indicate that current LLMs remain unsuitable for independent clinical use, reinforcing the need for expert oversight.
evidence.sample_unit: AI-generated visceral aneurysm clinical scenarios and responses

evidence.title: Speaking Patient's Language: Assessment of Readability and Fidelity of Artificial Intelligence-Optimized Consent Forms
evidence.outcome: content fidelity of LLM-edited consent forms
evidence.effect: Mean F1 0.71 ± 0.26; precision 0.95 ± 0.06; recall 0.62 ± 0.16, indicating few hallucinations but frequent content omissions.
evidence.quote: The mean F1 score was 0.71 ± 0.26, with high precision (0.95 ± 0.06) but lower recall (0.62 ± 0.16), indicating few hallucinations but frequent content omissions.

evidence.title: Evaluation of AI-Generated Surgical Decision Aids for Pelvic Floor Disorders
evidence.outcome: Physician-rated accuracy of ChatGPT decision aids on 5-point Likert scale
evidence.effect: Accuracy was <4 (unfavorable) on 2 of 6 decision aid tools; approximately 30% of topics require accuracy improvements.
evidence.quote: However, approximately 30% of the topics require improvements to accuracy, while all tools could benefit from improved reliability and readability.
evidence.sample_unit: ChatGPT-generated decision aid tools (one per question)

evidence.title: An Evaluation of Six Artificial Intelligence Tools for Formulary Management
evidence.venue: Journal of the American College of Clinical Pharmacy : JACCP
evidence.outcome: Accuracy and completeness of AI-drafted monographs versus reference standards
evidence.effect: Initial broad prompts yielded vague, incomplete, or inaccurate responses across all tools; section-specific prompts improved quality.
evidence.quote: Initial broad prompts requesting complete monographs yielded responses that were vague, incomplete, or inaccurate across all tools.

evidence.title: Reliability and readability of five AI chatbots for concussion health advice across retrieval augmented and pretrained models
evidence.outcome: Output quality against Amsterdam Consensus reference standards via DISCERN, EQIP, GQS
evidence.effect: Quality varied by model: DISCERN 36.18–47.36, EQIP 52.73–65.00; GQS moderate to good (2.91–3.36) without significant differences (p=0.373).
evidence.quote: Kruskal–Wallis testing identified significant between-model differences for DISCERN ( H = 20.161, p = 0.0005, η 2 = 0.323), EQIP ( H = 20.432, p = 0.0004, η 2 = 0.329), and JAMA ( H = 40.350, p < 0.001, η 2 = 0.727).

evidence.title: Can Large Language Models Translate Spine Surgery Guidelines for Patients? A Pilot Validation Study Using AO Spine Recommendations for Degenerative Cervical Myelopathy
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of LLM outputs against guideline reference standard, graded by 3 spine surgeons
evidence.effect: Clinician-facing outputs mean 2.93±0.26 with no inaccurate outputs; patient-facing mean 2.33±0.72 with omissions of key details.
evidence.quote: Clinician-facing outputs were highly accurate (mean 2.93±0.26) with near-perfect agreement and no outputs graded as inaccurate.
evidence.sample_unit: guideline-derived clinical scenarios (each queried once for clinicians and once for patients)

evidence.title: A workflow utilizing general-purpose large language models for efficient structuring and data mining of bone scintigraphy narratives
evidence.outcome: Error rate and severity of LLM structured extraction versus expert ground truth
evidence.effect: Error rates: DeepSeek-R1 3.9% (n=15), GPT-o3 9.3%, DeepSeek-V3 12.0%, Gemini 2.5 Pro 14.8%; major errors comprised 35.1%-60.0% of each model's errors.
evidence.quote: DeepSeek-R1 exhibited the highest accuracy, with a total error rate of only 3.9% ( n = 15).

evidence.title: Evaluating Use of Chat-Generative Pretrained Transformer for Patient Education of Pelvic Floor Disorders
evidence.outcome: Expert-rated accuracy of ChatGPT responses about pelvic floor disorders
evidence.effect: Reviewers found content on average 86.71% accurate with 25% variation across responses; median quality 3 to 4 (fair to good).
evidence.quote: Expert reviewers found that content was on average 86.71% accurate with 25% variation across responses.
evidence.sample_unit: ChatGPT responses to common patient questions about pelvic floor disorders

evidence.title: Patient-friendly simplification and translation of neuroradiology impressions using artificial intelligence
evidence.outcome: Rates of omissions, hallucinations, imprecisions in LLM-simplified impressions vs originals by two radiologists
evidence.effect: Major omissions 0.5%, 2.0%, 5.5%; malignant hallucinations 0.5%, 0%, 1.0%; major imprecisions 1.5%, 1.0%, 6.0% for brain MRI, head CT, spine MRI.
evidence.quote: Major omissions occurred in 0.5% of brain MRI reports, 2.0% of head CT reports, and 5.5% of spine MRI reports.
evidence.sample_unit: neuroradiology reports (brain MRI, head CT, spine MRI); 60 impressions translated to Spanish

evidence.title: Assessing Large Language Models for Clinical Coding in Hand Surgery: Effect of Note Authorship, Prompt Design, and Diagnosis/Procedure Type
evidence.venue: The Journal of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons
evidence.outcome: LLM ICD-10 and CPT coding accuracy against ground-truth correct codes
evidence.effect: All LLMs better predicted CPT codes (91.5% correct) than ICD-10 codes (23.9% correct); ChatGPT 3.5 less accurate for ICD-10 than ChatGPT 4.0 or Gemini (P<0.0001).
evidence.quote: All LLMs better predicted CPT codes (91.5% correct) than ICD-10 codes (23.9% correct).

evidence.title: Evaluation of Commonly Utilized Artificial Intelligence Large Language Models in Optimizing Readability, Accuracy, and Comprehension of Orthopaedic Oncology Patient Educational Materials
evidence.venue: The Journal of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons
evidence.outcome: accuracy and comprehension of AI rewrites
evidence.effect: Google Gemini F1 0.986, range 0.765-0.986, with 100% comprehension; MetaAI was compromised below sixth grade.
evidence.quote: Google Gemini achieved the highest F1 score of 0.986 (range: 0.765-0.986) and 100% comprehension.

evidence.title: Large Language Model-Generated Patient Instructions for Prescriptions in Primary Health Care: Preclinical Algorithm Validation
evidence.outcome: Output accuracy and safety of LLM medication instructions rated by clinicians
evidence.effect: About 22.7% of instructions per model could lead to incorrect medication use; Llama3.1-8B scored lower than ChatGPT-4.0 on adequacy (5.39 vs 6.82).
evidence.quote: Instructions leading to incorrect use of the medication had similar frequency among the models(ChatGPT-4.0: n=15, 22.7%; Llama3.1-8B: n=19, 22.8%; Llama3.1-8B-RAG: n=19, 22.8%; chi-square test P=.71).
evidence.sample_unit: evaluations of LLM-generated instructions by 62 primary health care prescribers

evidence.title: Large language models and retrieval-augmented platforms for dental implant complications: A blinded, expert-rated benchmarking study
evidence.outcome: Hallucinations in general-purpose LLM outputs on dental implant complications rated by blinded experts
evidence.effect: Hallucination-free rates among general-purpose platforms ranged from 36.7% (Claude 4.5 Haiku) to 93.3% (GPT-5.4 Thinking; Qwen 3.5-Plus), a significant difference.
evidence.quote: Among general-purpose platforms, safe rates ranged from 56.7% (Claude 4.5 Haiku) to 86.7% (Perplexity) and hallucination-free rates from 36.7% (Claude 4.5 Haiku) to 93.3% (GPT-5.4 Thinking; Qwen 3.5-Plus), both significant (Cochran's Q, p < 0.01).

evidence.title: Bridging the outcome documentation gap in epilepsy surgery: Validating large language model agents for automated Engel and International League Against Epilepsy scoring from clinical notes
evidence.outcome: Exact agreement with adjudicated outcome scores
evidence.effect: Definition-based prompt: 56.5% Engel subclass and 60.6% ILAE exact agreement.
evidence.quote: The definition-based prompt achieved 56.5% exact Engel subclass agreement (95% CI = 49.0-63.7) and 60.6% exact ILAE agreement (95% CI = 53.1-67.6).

evidence.title: Evaluating the Pediatric Behavior Guidance of Students Based on Actual Clinical Transcripts Scored by Faculty and Large Language Models: Pilot Comparative Study
evidence.outcome: Agreement of LLM scores with human assessor reference scores
evidence.effect: Absolute agreement ICC vs human transcript scores was 0.729 (95% CI 0.475-0.859) for free LLM and 0.670 (95% CI 0.377-0.825) for paid LLM, moderate agreement.
evidence.quote: Comparing transcript scores with the free-to-use LLM's and paid LLM's scores yielded an absolute agreement intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.729 (95% CI 0.475-0.859; P<.001) and 0.670 (95% CI 0.377-0.825; P<.001), respectively, demonstrating moderate agreement.

evidence.title: Reproducibility of AI-generated antibiotic recommendations in standardised clinical scenarios: A proof-of-concept experimental study
evidence.outcome: Clinical correctness of antibiotic and duration recommendations rated by blinded infectious diseases specialists
evidence.effect: OpenEvidence correct antibiotic recommendations 54.8% vs ChatGPT 35.7% (P<0.001); fully correct combined responses 33.4% vs 19.0% (P<0.001).
evidence.quote: Despite lower reproducibility, OpenEvidence generated more correct antibiotic recommendations (54.8% vs 35.7%; P < 0.001) and more fully correct combined responses (33.4% vs 19.0%; P < 0.001).
evidence.sample_unit: model interactions (12 scenarios x 100 submissions x 2 tools)

evidence.title: Assessment of Large Language Models in Colorectal Cancer Multidisciplinary Tumor Board Decision-Making: A Retrospective Single-Center Comparison of Guideline-Integrated General-Purpose vs. Domain-Specialized Models
evidence.outcome: Unsafe or discordant treatment recommendations
evidence.effect: Gemini safe 83.7%; MedGemma safe 62.3% (T=0.0) and 62.7% (T=1.0), with higher potentially risky/harmful rates.
evidence.quote: In the safety assessment, Gemini 2.5 demonstrated the highest proportion of safe recommendations (83.7%), whereas MedGemma (T = 0.0: 62.3% and T = 1.0: 62.7%) showed higher rates of potentially risky and harmful recommendations.
evidence.sample_unit: colorectal cancer cases discussed at MTB

evidence.title: Prompt Architecture as a High-Impact Design Factor in Expert-Rated Clinical Documentation Quality: A Controlled Comparative Study in Inpatient Rehabilitation
evidence.outcome: Unsupported clinical phrases
evidence.effect: Clinically relevant phrases: 71.3% (849/1190) no hallucinations, 19.7% (234/1190) deductions, and 9.0% (107/1190) hallucinations.
evidence.quote: Overall, 71.3% (849/1190) of phrases were classified as containing no hallucinations, 19.7% (234/1190) as deductions, and 9.0% (107/1190) as hallucinations.
evidence.country: Not reported (national public hospitals; likely Spain)

evidence.title: Performance of large language models as an information resource on functional hypothalamic amenorrhea for patients and healthcare professionals
evidence.outcome: Accuracy and completeness of LLM answers to FHA questions versus expert ratings
evidence.effect: Patient-level accuracy: ChatGPT 4.0 9/11 (82%), ChatGPT 3.5 and Gemini 8/11 (73%). Clinician-level: OpenEvidence 15/15 (100%), ChatGPT 4.0 93%, Gemini 80%.
evidence.quote: Among clinician-level questions, OpenEvidence demonstrated perfect accuracy (15 of 15; 100%), compared with 93% for and 80% for ChatGPT 4.0 and Gemini.

evidence.title: Large Language Models and Retrieval-Augmented Platforms for the Diagnosis and Management of Periodontal Diseases: A Blinded Expert-Rated Comparative Study of 11 Systems
evidence.outcome: Proportion of responses with at least one parameter scored dangerous (<=2) by blinded periodontists
evidence.effect: At least one parameter scored dangerous (<=2) in 3.3%-46.7% of responses across platforms, despite mean composite scores of 3.28-4.86.
evidence.quote: At least one parameter scored dangerous (≤ 2) in 3.3%-46.7% of responses across platforms, despite mean composite scores (3.28-4.86) exceeding the rubric midpoint of 3.0.

evidence.title: Human-in-the-loop validation of a sequential multi-LLM medical education pipeline
evidence.outcome: False-negative rate for blocking errors among AI-passed flashcards versus pre-specified safety threshold
evidence.effect: Evaluation-level FNR for blocking errors 1.00% (95% CI 0.50-1.78%) among 1100 evaluations of 980 PASS cards, exceeding the 0.3% threshold; card-level 1.12%, majority-vote 0.82%.
evidence.quote: Among 1100 evaluations of 980 text-level PASS cards, the evaluation-level false-negative rate (FNR) for blocking errors was 1.00% (95% CI 0.50-1.78%), exceeding the pre-specified 0.3% safety threshold; card-level (1.12%) and majority-vote (0.82%) analyses converged.

evidence.title: Radiologist Detection of Deficiencies in LLM-Generated Patient Communications About Radiology Reports: A Multi-Reader Study
evidence.venue: Journal of imaging informatics in medicine
evidence.outcome: LLM answer deficiencies
evidence.effect: 113/1200 (9.4%) deficient; 18 clinically significant errors (1.5%); 95 incomplete/ambiguous responses (7.9%).
evidence.quote: Of 1200 answers, 113 (9.4%) were deficient by consensus, including 18 clinically significant errors (1.5%) and 95 incomplete/ambiguous responses (7.9%).
evidence.sample_unit: LLM-generated answers to simulated patient questions

evidence.title: A cross-sectional evaluation of Large Language Model answers to dental questions
evidence.outcome: Harmfulness of LLM dental answers rated by two dentists
evidence.effect: Without a system prompt, 56% of outputs from gpt-4o, gpt-4o-mini, and llama-3.3-70b were classified as harmful (pooled across both languages).
evidence.quote: Without a system prompt, 56% of outputs from gpt-4o, gpt-4o-mini, and llama-3.3-70b were classified as harmful (pooling both languages; a question was counted as harmful if at least one of its five generated answers was labeled harmful by at least one annotator).

evidence.title: Assessing the accuracy of ChatGPT responses to caregiver questions in pediatric neurology: an observational study
evidence.outcome: Accuracy and comprehensiveness of ChatGPT answers to pediatric neurology caregiver questions, rated by two neurologists
evidence.effect: 60.95% (64/105) comprehensive; 31.43% (33/105) correct but incomplete; 3.8% (4/105) fully incorrect.
evidence.quote: 60.95%(64/105) of responses were rated as comprehensive, while 31.43%(33/105) were correct but incomplete; fully incorrect responses were uncommon 3.8%(4/105).

evidence.title: ChatGPT improves readability in validated spine patient-reported outcome measures
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of AI-revised PROMs against original validated instruments as reference
evidence.effect: 59.7% of revised PROMs had at least one error versus the original instrument; most common errors were altered response scales (23%), omitted timeframes (18%), merged items (16%).
evidence.quote: The most common errors involved alteration or removal of validated response scales (23%), omission or simplification of key time frames (18%), and inappropriate combination of multiple items into a single prompt (16%).

evidence.title: Optimizing GPT-5 for Operation-Procedure-Code-Extraction from Operative Reports in Meningioma Surgery: Feasibility and Comparison of Context-Enhancements
evidence.outcome: Inaccurate GPT-5 OPS code output versus in-hospital ground-truth coding
evidence.effect: Unenhanced GPT-5 achieved only 44% correct coding, with 132 total mistakes, 105 hallucinations, 9% chaotic LLM failure, and 26% vital mistakes.
evidence.quote: GPT-5s and GPT-5o showed identical accuracy (44/100 correct codes), followed by GPT-5e (70/100) and GPT-5r (79/100).

evidence.title: Correctness, Harmfulness, and Diversity of Large Language Models for Colonoscopy Preparation Assistance: Comparative Evaluation Study
evidence.outcome: AI Coach response correctness and harmful errors vs prep instructions reference standard
evidence.effect: Human-rated turn-level accuracy: o3 93.5%, GPT-4.1 90.8%, Llama 78.1%, Mistral 68.1%; all models produced harmful errors (o3 11/17 errors harmful).

commentary.bottom_line: Seventy-one studies apply reference-standard evaluation to AI outputs and find accuracy that varies widely by task and model, and in several studies automated and expert methods disagreed on what counts as an error. No study tests whether evaluation before deployment reduces patient harm or whether predefined organizational risk tolerances change deployment decisions.

perspectives.view: Among the summarized tests, three are level 2 prospective real-deployment comparisons, one is a level 3 real-deployment pre-post study without a comparator, and the rest are offline level 4 designs. Precision was 0.33 for trial matching, while field accuracy for RCT summaries ranged from 85.4% to 97.9%. No study compares evaluated with unevaluated deployment, so certainty is very low.

Expert review flagged five potentially dangerous chatbot responses in one study and placed 4.2% of responses in the lowest safety category in another. Hazard studies report harmful plans in 16% of infectious disease cases and high harm risk in 26% of drug answers. Evaluation can detect errors, but no study shows it stopped errors from reaching patients.

Evaluation methods did not always agree. Automated completeness correlated with expert usability at rho ≈ 0.393, and relevance metrics correlated weakly or negatively with correctness. An automated checking tool found 1 error in 2,067 checks while raters found soft errors in 32% of briefs. A judge LLM reached AC1=0.80 with experts. Layered methods may capture different error types.

Reference standards require expert labor. One team annotated 50 of 4,762 notes as ground truth, which suggests evaluation on samples may be feasible. Another reached 93.6% agreement only on the fourth iteration after early scores as low as 0.26, which implies repeated evaluation cycles and staff time before deployment.

Three tests involved non-English or translation settings, including layered evaluation of translated discharge instructions, extraction from Chinese records, and scoring of German patient records. One study extracted housing instability from notes of pregnant women. No test reported Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations, so the performance of evaluation methods in those groups is unknown.

NIST AI 600-1 advises comparing output with ground truth using several methods, and CHAI playbooks tie project pathways to risk category. No supplied study sets or tests a predefined organizational risk tolerance, so the threshold component of this recommendation rests on framework consensus rather than empirical tests.

In one study otolaryngologists rated ChatGPT empathy at 4.28 of 5 but accuracy at 3.76 and flagged five responses as potentially dangerous. Patients may trust fluent answers that contain errors, which suggests evaluations should score accuracy and safety separately from tone.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares AI deployments that underwent benchmarked, multi-method evaluation against predefined risk thresholds with deployments that did not, using patient harm or error interception as outcomes. Studies are also needed that validate automated and LLM-as-judge methods against clinician review across tasks, that report how organizations set risk tolerances, and that measure the staff time and cost of building reference standards.
commentary.underserved_note: Three tests included non-English or limited English proficiency settings (translated discharge instructions, Chinese eCRF extraction, German patient records), and one assessed housing instability in notes from pregnant women. No test reported Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations, so health systems serving those patients cannot assume that reference standards or error rates from these studies transfer and may need evaluation samples drawn from their own populations.
